name: module
intent: Partition the domain model into cohesive, named units whose names come from the domain, so that each unit can be understood and changed with minimal reference to the rest of the system.
problem: As a model grows, code gets grouped by whatever is convenient at the time - by technical layer, file type or framework convention - and the concepts of one domain area end up scattered over the codebase. Readers can no longer see which concepts belong together, every change ripples through unrelated packages, and nothing in the code tells a domain expert what the model contains.
context: Any codebase whose domain model is larger than a handful of concepts and whose language offers a grouping mechanism (package, namespace, module, compilation unit) - greenfield, where boundaries are chosen for the first time, and legacy, where a technical layout must be re-partitioned along domain seams. Applies inside one bounded context and per context when several share a repository.
benefits: Comprehension: a reader can study one module as a self-contained subsystem; modules are the chapters of the model's story and cross-references between them stay minimal.
Module names become part of the ubiquitous language: Billing, Shipping, Orders are what developers and domain experts say in conversations, tests, tickets and error messages.
Low coupling shrinks the blast radius of change: a change internal to one module does not force edits in unrelated modules, so refactoring and review stay local.
One place to hide implementation: the module publishes a narrow interface (public, exported, __all__) and everything else stays internal, so clients depend on the concept rather than its mechanics.
Independent ownership: a module can be owned, reviewed and tested by one team and later split into its own deliverable or service without redesigning the model.
Surfaces model defects: if a concept cannot be placed in any module, or forces a cycle, the model - not the packaging - is usually wrong.
tradeoffs: Boundaries are sticky: the partition leaks into imports, build definitions, artifact names, test paths and documentation, so a later re-partition is a wide mechanical change and a published module cannot be moved without breaking consumers.

Conceptual cohesion fights technical cohesion: a domain concept often needs collaborators that are not domain concepts (persistence, transport, serialization), so you either let the module depend outward or split the concept across modules - one of the two cohesion senses always loses.

Cycles have to be resolved by hand: when two modules genuinely need each other you must merge them, invert one dependency through an interface or event, or accept a cycle. Toolchains differ sharply - Go rejects import cycles outright while Java and Python accept them silently - so the guarantee is only as strong as the language.

Granularity drifts quietly in both directions: too coarse and the module becomes a second global namespace, too fine and internals leak across many tiny modules while the dependency graph explodes. Nothing in the compiler complains.

Enforcement is uneven: strong mechanisms (JPMS, C++20 modules, Go internal/, Rust pub(crate)) buy real guarantees at the cost of build complexity, whereas package- and namespace-only layouts are convention and erode the first time someone deep-imports an internal.
Module boundaries become team boundaries: re-partitioning later rearranges ownership, review paths and release trains, not only files.

participants.responsibility: The cohesive unit itself: a named set of model concepts belonging to one area of the domain; it owns its internals and is the unit other modules refer to.

The deliberately small subset of the module other modules may use - exported or public declarations, an explicit export list, a documented public API - and therefore the only legal dependency surface.

Everything the module does not publish: helpers, data structures, persistence and transport details, hidden by whatever mechanism the language offers (internal, package-private, static, unexported, non-exported).
The modules that depend on this one through its published interface only; their imports are what a cycle check examines and what keeps the boundary honest.

use_cases: An e-commerce model split into Orders, Billing, Shipping and Catalog packages, each holding its entities, value objects, domain services and repository interfaces.
Re-partitioning a layered /controllers /services /models codebase into domain modules without changing its observable behaviour.
One module per bounded context inside a shared repository, with each context's published surface as the only cross-context import path.
A shared kernel or domain library in which the published interface of each module is a versioned API consumed by other teams.
A C++20 modules or JPMS build in which illegal dependencies are rejected at compile time instead of being caught in review.
Preparing a monolith for extraction: modules first, independent deployment later, so the split follows the model rather than the build graph.
Hexagonal/ports-and-adapters isolation: domain modules publish only port interfaces; adapters live in separate modules that depend inward, so the domain stays framework-agnostic.
Event-driven microservices boundaries: each module publishes domain events as its only cross-module interface, keeping coupling at the event-contract level rather than the call graph.
A library with an explicit public API surface (a shallow hub module over internal implementation packages) so consumers upgrade safely while internals churn.
Monorepo per-context ownership: each team owns a module's published interface; the CI gate enforces that no import crosses a team boundary without going through a published contract.

NestJS modular monolith: each NestJS module is a bounded context with its own domain, application, and infrastructure layers; cross-module communication uses EventEmitterModule for in-process events and NestJS Microservices (TCP) for future service extraction.

.NET modular monolith: each bounded context is a separate assembly (e.g., Ordering.Domain, Ordering.Contracts, Ordering.Infrastructure) with Contracts as the only permitted cross-module reference; architecture tests (ArchUnit) enforce that runtime assemblies never reference each other directly.

Laravel DDD vertical modules: each module (Order, Payment, Customer) is a self-contained vertical slice with Domain/, Application/, and Infrastructure/ subdirectories; a ddd:check artisan command validates that Domain never imports Laravel, HTTP, or Infrastructure classes.

Nx/TypeScript monorepo with scope tags: libs/ are tagged scope:<product> or scope:shared; @nx/enforce-module-boundaries ESLint rule prevents cross-scope imports except through published contracts, enforcing that apps never import other apps directly.

Spring Modulith application: Spring Boot application carved into modules matching bounded contexts; ApplicationModules.verify() runs as a build gate to reject illegal inter-module dependencies; @TransactionalEventListener enforces transactional event publishing across module boundaries.

Go monorepo with nested internal packages: each bounded context (catalog, inventory, order) has its own nested internal/ directory; Go's internal-package rule prevents cross-context imports at compile time; contexts communicate through public-facing port/ and event/ packages outside the internal tree.

Go Workspaces for independent bounded contexts: each bounded context is its own go.mod; go.work enables simultaneous local editing; context boundaries are module-level rather than directory-level, enabling independent CI pipelines and deployment per context.

Outbox-pattern module boundary: the module owning an aggregate also owns its outbox table and outboxpublisher; other modules consume events through the outbox, never directly from the aggregate, keeping the data ownership boundary clean and enabling at-least-once delivery.
Spring Modulith: ApplicationModules.verify() treats application modules as an acyclic graph, rejects cycles, and restricts cross-module access to published API packages.
Java Platform Module System (JPMS): group cohesive packages into a module, declare explicit requires dependencies, and export only the packages intended for clients.
Nx workspace: tag applications and libraries with scopes, then enforce dependency constraints so feature modules can depend on approved shared modules without importing one another.
avoid_when: The model is small (a handful of concepts, one team): a flat package or namespace, or even a single package, is simpler and cheaper to keep correct.
Prototypes and throwaway scripts: a domain partition nobody will maintain adds ceremony without adding comprehension.

The language or framework already fixes the layout (Rails app/, .NET project templates, Android feature modules): follow the host convention and express the model through names instead of building a parallel hierarchy.
The real need is translation at a system boundary rather than internal organisation: an anti-corruption layer or a facade is the right structure there.
The code is one cohesive algorithm (a specification, pipeline or parser) rather than a model of several concepts: splitting it further separates what should stay together.
anti_patterns: Layer-driven packaging: /controllers, /services, /models (or .ui, .business, .data) scatter every domain concept so that no module tells a story.
The catch-all module: common, shared, helpers or a single 'domain' package that everything imports and that imports everything - a namespace in name only.
Hierarchy theatre: deep artificial nesting (com.acme.app.domain.model.impl.v2) that mirrors the org chart or framework internals instead of domain concepts.
Boundary by convention only: imports run in circles, every change still touches several 'modules', and the structure is asserted in documentation rather than in the dependency graph.
Pass-through modules: a module or barrel file that only re-exports another module wholesale, adding a hop and hiding which concepts actually belong together.

The 'utils' anti-pattern: a domain-agnostic package that accumulates unrelated helpers - becomes an import magnet, cannot be tested in isolation, and resists refactoring because everything depends on it.

Entity-based modules: giving each entity (Order, OrderItem, OrderLineItem) its own package creates chatty, fine-grained modules where a single use case touches five modules; group related entities by business capability instead.

One-giant module: stuffing an entire subdomain into a single module with 15-20 entities hides internal conceptual boundaries and makes the module harder to understand than the original flat structure; split by subdomain or aggregate root instead.

Technical modules: packaging by layer (/domain, /application, /infrastructure per entity) recreates the scattering problem with extra indirection - modules should be organized around business capability, not technical role.

Circular context dependencies: two bounded contexts that reference each other's internal types directly violate the ADP and make independent deployment impossible; resolve through domain events, shared interfaces owned by the consuming context, or a shared kernel.
design_principles: High cohesion and low coupling in the conceptual sense: modules group concepts that are understood and changed together and depend on as few other modules as possible.
Information hiding: publish a narrow interface, keep everything else internal, and let clients depend on the concept rather than its implementation.
Naming as design: module names are part of the ubiquitous language - if a module cannot be named with a domain term, the boundary or the model is wrong.
Single responsibility at module level: one module, one coherent area of the model.
Acyclic dependencies: module dependencies should form a directed graph without cycles, which is what keeps modules independently comprehensible.
Acyclic Dependencies Principle (ADP): allow no cycles in the package-dependency graph; break cycles by extracting an interface, inverting a dependency through an event, or merging the modules.

Stable Dependencies Principle (SDP): depend in the direction of stability; unstable modules (those that change often) should depend on stable modules (architecture, high-level policy), not the reverse.

Stable Abstractions Principle (SAP): a module should be as abstract as it is stable; stable modules contain abstract types (interfaces, abstract classes) that can be extended; volatile modules can be more concrete.
best_practices: Name modules after domain concepts, never after technical layers or file types; read the resulting structure aloud - if it does not sound like the domain, redo it.
Keep concepts that change together in the same module; put non-domain collaborators (adapters, DTOs, ORM mapping) either inside as internal details or outside behind an interface.
Publish deliberately: maintain an explicit export list (public API, exports, __all__, pub use) and keep the published surface as small as clients allow.
Measure coupling and watch for cycles: if two modules always change together, merge them; if a module needs a foreign concept, move the concept or introduce a published interface.

Re-partition as the model deepens: module boundaries are refactorable design decisions, revisited whenever domain understanding changes; refine the model until it partitions along high-level domain concepts.
Choose the weakest enforcement mechanism that gives the boundary you need, and upgrade to language-level modules only when the build can pay for it.
Apply the Acyclic Dependencies Principle: run a cycle-detection check in CI; treat any import cycle as a build-breaking defect, not a code-smell-to-fix-later.
Make module names part of the ubiquitous language: if developers and domain experts cannot say the module name naturally in conversation, the boundary does not reflect the domain.

Treat the published interface as a versioned API contract: once exported, a name costs more to rename than to keep; avoid exporting internals that will need to change independently of the module's concept.
Assign module ownership to one team: a module without a clear owner becomes a meeting point for too many concerns and erodes toward a catch-all; team assignment keeps boundaries honest.

Enforce boundaries in CI, not in documentation: use architecture testing tools (ArchUnit, import-linter, dependency-cruiser, ESLint @nx/enforce-module-boundaries) as build gates; a boundary that only lives in a wiki is a suggestion, not a rule.

Validate boundaries with the change test: ask 'if I change this business rule, which modules are affected?' A well-designed module boundary means the answer is exactly one module; if multiple modules must change for one business concept, the boundary is wrong.

Give each module its own data schema or database: no shared tables across module boundaries; a module reads its own data only through its published interface, not by reaching into another module's storage.

Use one-way dependencies always: if module A needs something from module B, A defines the interface and B implements it (Dependency Inversion Principle); the interface lives in A's published surface, never in B's internals.

In a monorepo, treat shared packages as versioned APIs: the bigger a shared package and the faster it changes, the more it couples every consumer; keep shared packages small, slow-changing, and with a stable contract.

Nest internal/ directories per bounded context in Go: place domain, application, and infrastructure packages inside a context-specific internal/ tree so Go's internal-package rule enforces access control at compile time, not convention.

Restrict cross-module communication to events and published interfaces: synchronous calls between modules tend to create tight coupling; prefer domain events for reactions and published interfaces for queries, so modules can evolve and deploy independently.

Document the module's public surface as rigorously as an external API: a new developer should be able to use a module correctly by reading only its published interface; anything not published is an implementation detail subject to change without notice.

Vaughn Vernon, Implementing Domain-Driven Design, Addison-Wesley (2013), Chapter 9 'Modules' - module naming conventions, module placement within and across bounded contexts.

Alexander Molochko, 'DDD Bounded Contexts and Java Modules', Baeldung (2020) - practical JPMS (Java 9 Module System) example mapping bounded contexts to Java modules with exports, requires, provides, and uses directives.
Stephen Colebourne, 'Java SE 9 - JPMS module naming', blog.joda.org (2017) - reverse-DNS module naming convention, module-as-package-aggregate design rationale, and hidden-package management.
Real Python, 'Python __all__: Packages, Modules, and Wildcard Imports' (2024) - __all__ as the explicit public interface declaration, best practices for package-level export control.
PEP 842 (Python), 'Module Exports' (peps.python.org) - proposed export statement and __export__ variable for explicit module surface declaration in Python.
Segflow, 'The case against helper packages named utils' (2025) - utils/shared/common package anti-pattern analysis: import magnet, anti-cohesion, untestable culture, and the refactoring approach.

Manoel Medeiros, 'Acyclic Dependencies Principle: from monolith to microservice, from graph theory to the cost of change' (2026) - ADP applied to bounded contexts, microservices, monorepos, and polyrepos; event-driven acyclicity, inversion techniques, and the ADP-SDP-SAP trio.

Encore.dev, 'Microservices in a Monorepo: Structure, Shared Code, and When It Fits' (2026) - monorepo vs polyrepo tradeoffs, shared-package discipline, graph-aware CI (Turborepo, Nx, Bazel), and preventing hidden coupling through explicit published interfaces.

Pavan Rangani, 'Modular Monolith: The Architecture Between Monolith and Microservices' (2026) - modular monolith design principles, boundary enforcement (Spring Modulith, architecture tests), one-schema-per-module, event-driven inter-module communication, and incremental extraction path to microservices.

Milan Jovanovic, 'Module Boundaries With Bounded Contexts in Modular Monolith' (2026) - change-test validation, entity-based vs capability-based modules, Contracts assembly pattern in .NET, cross-context communication via events and shared interfaces.

Stéphane Erard, 'Part VI: Create Bounded Context Libraries' (serard.dev, 2026) - DDD bounded context library design in C#/.NET with Onion Architecture; zero-outward-dependency domain projects, compiler-enforced dependency rules, SharedKernel extraction, and DbContext-per-context migration.

Matheus Paiva et al., 'An Empirical Study of Cohesion and Coupling: Balancing Optimisation and Disruption' (UCL CS, 2016) - largest longitudinal study (233 releases, 10 systems) showing developers respect cohesion/coupling metrics but 57% structural disruption prevents adoption of automated re-modularisation; multiobjective approach finds 22% cohesion improvement within developer-tolerated disruption.

G. Bavota et al., 'An empirical study on the developers' perception of software coupling' (ICSE 2013) - 80 participants from 9 countries showing developers perceive conceptual cohesion (class responsibilities) as more intuitive than structural cohesion metrics, validating concept-level modularisation over mechanical metrics.

AWS Prescriptive Guidance, 'Building hexagonal architectures on AWS' (aws.amazon.com) - hexagonal architecture as DDD enabler, domain as centre, ports and adapters pattern, CQRS within bounded contexts, and recommended folder structure for entrypoints/domain/adapters separation.

SamuelNunesDev, 'Laravel DDD Toolkit' (github.com/SamuelNunesDev/laravel-ddd-toolkit) - vertical module structure for Laravel combining domain capability grouping with hexagonal ports-and-adapters inside each module; ddd:check validates hexagonal rules in CI.

Rust Language Reference, 'Visibility and Privacy' (doc.rust-lang.org, 2024) - pub, pub(crate), pub(super), pub(in path) visibility modifiers; crate-root re-exports; pub use for API facade; privacy-checking pass enforcement.

Software Patterns Lexicon, 'Module Privacy Pattern in Rust' (softwarepatternslexicon.com, 2024) - using Rust's visibility modifiers to expose a compact documented API while keeping representation, helper functions, and coordination logic private; re-export facade pattern; pub(crate) for internal cross-module collaboration.

Go Language Authors, 'Organizing a Go module' (go.dev/doc/modules/layout, 2026) - internal/ directory for non-exportable packages, cmd/ for commands, multi-package module layout, and go.work for workspace-level monorepo management.

zenn.dev/135yshr, 'Implementing Bounded Contexts in Go Module Architecture' (2026) - nested internal/ per bounded context for compiler-enforced isolation, Go Workspaces for module-level independence, shared-interface vs domain-event inter-context communication patterns.
